content:
The 2026 award winners at The Wine Communicator Awards, holding Brendan Carter. Image supplied

Last night, Brendan Carter from Bottleshock was named the 2026 Wine Communicator of the Year by Wine Communicators of Australia (WCA).

The announcement was the culmination of the celebrations at WCA’s sold out annual Awards Night in Sydney, with Brendan accepting his award from WCA National Chair, Lynda Schenk.

“The Wine Communicator Awards are a highlight of the year for our community,” said Schenk.

“From digital campaigns and events, to journalism, education, research, hospitality and advocacy, the awards celebrate the individuals and organisations helping connect people with wine through compelling stories, fresh ideas and meaningful conversations.

“The Wine Communicator of the Year, Brendan Carter, demonstrates an exceptional ability to engage consumers through his Bottleshock.TV and The Big Blind League wine tasting competition while also challenging us all to act differently in how we talk about wine. His fresh thinking, willingness to challenge convention, and commitment to building stronger connections between wine and consumers make him a truly deserving recipient of this honour.”

Upon being named the winner, Carter said commanding people’s attention is a privilege.

“The most important thing when it comes to building audiences is trust and authenticity and that is where Australia has a unique opportunity. Very few accents click in people’s minds globally as the Australian one. The ability to command attention is becoming scarcer but if we can establish Australian accents globally as the authority on wine now, we might just be okay,” he said.

The annual Wine Communicator Awards recognise outstanding excellence in wine communication in all its forms.

33 experienced and respected industry professionals judged entries across 13 different categories. The judges were hugely impressed with the calibre of creativity, passion and skill shown across a wide range of communication channels.

Toasts were also made to the 13 category winners with trophy-winning wines from this year’s Sydney Royal Wine Awards.

The 2026 Wine Communicator Awards category winners are as follows:

Best Australian Wine Communication Campaign, sponsored by Wine Australia

  • Jacob’s Creek x Australian Open 2026 by Vinarchy

Best Digital Communication, sponsored by Liquid Ideas

  • BottleShock by Brendan Carter, Noah Ward and Henry Doyle.

Best Social Media Communication, sponsored by Endeavour Group

Brokenwood Wines

Best Published Feature Article or Wine Column, sponsored by De Bortoli Wines

  • Campbell Mattinson for his article ‘Peter Dredge is not a winemaker by accident’

Best Wine Packaging Design, sponsored by WineHub

  • Poco Vino, designed by Australian Vintage

Best New Wine Book, sponsored by Adelaide University

  • Penfolds Rewards of Patience, Andrew Caillard MW + Longueville Media

Best Winery Website, sponsored by Parallax Design

  • Henschke

Best Wine-Themed Event, sponsored by Purple Giraffe

MOULD x Pinot Palooza

Best Wine Communicator: Cellar Door, sponsored by Coravin

  • Rhiannan Wilson, former Dandelion Vineyard

Best Wine Communicator: Marketing, sponsored by Vinomofo

  • Lara Apollonio, Sidewood Estate

Best Wine Communicator: Sales, sponsored by Coravin

  • Roger Bond, Dan Murphy’s Double Bay

Best Wine Educator, sponsored by RIEDEL

  • Yvonne Hilsz, Positive Change Coaching

Best Wine Student, sponsored by Wine Communicators of Australia

  • Alexandra Quinton

Overall Winner ~ 2026 Wine Communicator of the Year

  • Brendan Carter

content:
LTR: Tom Bartholomaeus and Nigel Blieschke of Torbreck Vintners

By Kyra Trussell

Last Thursday, a well-attended workshop discussing and demonstrating reworking old vine Grenache was held in the Barossa Valley.

Hosted by The Barossa Viticulture Technical Group (BVTG) and led by technical viticulturist Tom Bartholomaeus as well as chief viticulturist Nigel Blieschke of Torbreck Vintners, the morning led attendees through three blocks of Grenache vines.

The first block had been successfully reworked in 2020 with an approximate 95% strike rate. Shoot thinning had been performed at this site to manage vine density, prevent clumping and improve airflow.

“If you look at the shadow of these vines, there’s dappled light. That’s a really good indicator of the quality of Grenache,” Blieschke said of the first block.

The second block was reworked two years later in 2022 with a 75% strike rate, which Bartholomaeus said was a disappointing result.

He went on to explain that, compared to the first block, the second site was around 1.3 tonne to the hectare lower in yields.

“We just struggled to get things growing, so a lot of the cordons are a bit shorter. We’re still trying to extend them in places, just with regard to how we do that in a in a soft pruning practice.

“We’ll always kind of go halfway with putting a new cordon down, leave a shoot from a downward facing bud, and we’ll extend that in the second year to ensure that we get really good growth on our shoots as we go.

“That’s been a far lengthier process in here, and the depth is something that’s held us back as well. So, we thought that we could speed up the process, and you’ll see that the shoot length in here probably isn’t as good either — that’s because we find that our trunks are just a little bit weaker too. We just got a little bit too excited,” Bartholomaeus reflected.

Blieschke emphasised to the attendees that there was an important lesson to learn from the second block.

“None of this is short-term, you’ve got to be prepared to do the work over time…slow and steady rather than flat out, take your time,” he urged.

The third block was a yet to be reworked project for 2026 which Bartholomaeus described as “a combination of the lessons that we’ve learned in other bits and pieces that we’ve done”.

“We want to give it a year or two to see if we can push some material down low to begin with. I think [with] vine number two,” he gestured to the second vine in the row, “we’ve got success in that we had a water shoot that was growing down low and were able to cut off the top end of the vine, and that’s good to go — that’s a vine that we’ll consider starting the spur pruning journey on next year, but we’ve also left material.”

“Do you prioritise future or fruit? That’s the question,” Blieschke added.

“A lot of knowledge from Europe would say if you’re going for future, don’t go for fruit. This one is for the future. When we are pruning those vines, our pruners are thinking about if they’re all growing together, they’re looking to not grow together,” he explained to the audience.

Guests were given the opportunity to inspect multiple soil pits across the three vineyards, which were created to showcase what viticulturists should look for in healthy Grenache root system growths and to discuss the irrigation requirements of the vines.

A standout piece of advice from the event was the benefits Torbreck had found from using the same four pruners for 10 years.

Bartholomaeus told of how they save time and effort not having to reteach the intricacies of each vineyard by bringing back a team who knows the blocks well.

Longevity was an overarching theme at the workshop, with the two viticulturists demonstrating how they will rework the third vineyard with pruning and a saw to prioritise the future health of the vines.

The workshop ended with SARDI research scientist Tarita Furlan presenting the latest research on preventing and managing Eutypa.

title: Stanley Wine Bar wins three major accolades at 2026 Tasmanian Wine List of the Year Awards
summary:
Stanley Wine Bar has emerged as the standout of the 2026 Tasmanian Wine List of the Year Awards, taking home three major accolades, including the coveted Overall Judges' Choice Best Tasmanian Wine List of the Year. The north-west coast gem also claimed Best Small Bar Wine List and, “proving the public agrees with the experts”, the People's Choice Award. Presented by Wine Tasmania, the annual awards “recognise the restaurants, bars and hospitality venues going above and beyond to showcase the quality, diversity and downright deliciousness of Tasmanian wine”. Wine Tasmania CEO Sheralee Davies congratulated this year’s award winners.

content:
Stanley Wine Bar claimed three major accolades, including the Overall Judges’ Choice Best Tasmanian Wine List of the Year. Image supplied

Stanley Wine Bar has emerged as the standout of the 2026 Tasmanian Wine List of the Year Awards, taking home three major accolades, including the coveted Overall Judges’ Choice Best Tasmanian Wine List of the Year.

The north-west coast gem also claimed Best Small Bar Wine List and, “proving the public agrees with the experts”, the People’s Choice Award.

The judges also awarded the following venues:

Overall Judges’ Choice Best Tasmanian Wine List of the Year:

  • Stanley Wine Bar

Judges’ Choice Best Tasmanian Wine List – Launceston:

  • Stillwater Restaurant
  • Highly Commended: Grain of the Silos

Judges’ Choice Best Tasmanian Wine List – Hobart:

  • Mures Upper Deck

Judges’ Choice Best Tasmanian Wine List – Regional:

  • Homestead at Piermont Retreat

Judges’ Choice Best Tasmanian Wine List – Small Bar:

  • Stanley Wine Bar
  • Highly Commended: Bar Clarry

People’s Choice Best Tasmanian Wine List of the Year:

  • Stanley Wine Bar

Presented by Wine Tasmania, the annual awards “recognise the restaurants, bars and hospitality venues going above and beyond to showcase the quality, diversity and downright deliciousness of Tasmanian wine”.

Wine Tasmania CEO Sheralee Davies congratulated this year’s award winners.

“On behalf of our talented wine producers, we are thrilled to recognise the legendary support of venues for our local wines. From small to large, from regional and major towns right around the island, this year has seen some incredible wine lists and efforts to champion our local wines.

“We know people are increasingly travelling to Tasmania to explore our wonderful wines and visit our regional cellar doors. We want visitors and locals alike to enjoy the quality and diversity of Tassie wine when they sit down at a restaurant, pull up a stool at a bar, ask for a recommendation or the stories behind the wines,” she said.

This year’s awards were assessed by a judging panel comprising of Curly Haslam-Coates of Vintage Tasmania, internationally recognised wine communicator Cassandra Camerer-Charlick and respected wine journalist as well as critic Nola James, alongside Wine Tasmania.

“We congratulate and thank every winner, highly commended venue and each finalist for their commitment to putting Tassie wine in the spotlight. We also thank our voluntary judges for generously sharing their time and expertise,” Davies said.

“Given Tasmania’s ever-growing global reputation for some of the best cool climate wines on the planet, celebrating and sharing these at home in Tasmania makes perfect sense.”

Coinciding with the announcement of the 2026 Tasmanian Wine List of the Year Awards, Wine Tasmania said it is delighted to unveil the new 2027 Tasmanian Wine Trails Guide.

“Featuring a refreshed look and feel, the latest edition is the perfect companion for exploring Tasmania’s diverse wine trails, exceptional producers and unique cellar door experiences,” the organisations said.

“Wine is a key motivation for people to travel to Tasmania and visit our regional cellar doors. This visitor segment stays longer, spends more and travels further into our regions than other visitor segments,” Davies added.

title: SIMEI reveals winners of Lucio Mastroberadino Innovation Challenge
summary:
SIMEI has announced the winners of its Lucio Mastroberardino Innovation Challenge, designed to honour “the most interesting innovations for the wine and beverage supply chain”. The 2026 edition of the challenge sees four Technology Innovation Awards, four Green Innovation Awards and 12 New Technology mentions. The awards are to be officially given on Tuesday, 17 November during the inaugural ceremony of the 31st edition of the SIMEI international exhibition for winemaking and bottling machinery. The winners were determined by a technical-scientific committee composed of university professors, technicians and representatives of user companies.

The post SIMEI reveals winners of Lucio Mastroberadino Innovation Challenge appeared first on Winetitles.
content:
The CR Racing Press by L.A.S.I, which has received a New Technology Award. Image supplied

SIMEI has announced the winners of its Lucio Mastroberardino Innovation Challenge, designed to honour “the most interesting innovations for the wine and beverage supply chain”.

The 2026 edition of the challenge sees four Technology Innovation Awards, four Green Innovation Awards and 12 New Technology mentions. The awards are to be officially given on Tuesday, 17 November during the inaugural ceremony of the 31st edition of the SIMEI international exhibition for winemaking and bottling machinery. The winners were determined by a technical-scientific committee composed of university professors, technicians and representatives of user companies.

Technology Innovation Awards

  • The “concrete balance between quality, efficiency, flexibility and sustainability” earned the Elyra project by Bertolaso of Omnia Technologies the top award. Organisers explained that Elyra is a bottling system designed to reduce water use and simplify maintenance.
  • Disgorging Valve by Gai Macchine was recognised for its “design ingenuity” and is a multifunction valve used in sparkling wine production.
  • IntraSense and MetaFerm by HTS Enologia (Luigi Scavone) was awarded for intelligent fermentation control.
  • Virtual5 by Omnia Technologies received the award for its contribution in terms of “vision, research and the ability to transform technology into value for the industry”.

Green Innovation Awards

  • Flavy FGCM by Bucher Vaslin was recognised for its commitment to sustainability. It is a filtration system that processes musts and young wines with high levels of suspended solids while reducing water and energy use.
  • GoLo Wine De-alcoholation System by Logichem uses vacuum evaporation with an integrated heat pump and reportedly reduces power consumption by 70%.
  • Altair by Astro is a capsule designed to make it easier to separate aluminium from glass before recycling.
  • Virtuo by Crealis Group is a capsule made from 100% recycled tin that is said to maintain traditional performance while reducing production-cycle CO₂ emissions by 61%.

New Technology Awards

  • Enovision by 3U Vision — An optical grape sorting system powered by AI.
  • Stiratura Universale by Acmi Labelling (Omnia Technologies) — A label finishing system.
  • LiOX VT by Diam Bouchage — A technical closure designed for still wines.
  • Ekinsa App by Equipamientos Industriales Ekinsa — A digital system for controlling the washing and sterilisation of barriques.
  • CR Racing Press by L.A.S.I. — A press designed for processing whole or crushed grapes.
  • AMHS System by Nortan (Omnia Technologies) — A modular system for capsulating machines.
  • Smart Valve System by Parsec — A temperature control system for winemaking.
  • Pop Guard Safety Ring — A cork retention system designed for sparkling wines.
  • Clear Flow by Puleo — A flotation system for musts.
  • Pressatura Pulse by Puleo — A technology developed for pneumatic wine presses.
  • Nomasense CO2 C2000 by Vinventions — An instrument that measures dissolved CO₂ in wine.
  • Winegrid DataDriven by Watgrid (Winegrid) — An AI-powered digital monitoring platform.

title: 90% of Barossa vineyard area now participating in national sustainability program
summary:
Barossa Australia has revealed that more than 300 Barossa vineyards and wineries are now participating in Sustainable Winegrowing Australia, with over 80% achieving independent certification. 12,768 Ha (90%) of Barossa’s 14,162 Ha under-vine is participating in Sustainable Winegrowing Australia — a 1,264 hectare (10%) increase on the previous year. 303 Barossa vineyards and wineries are now members of the program (an increase of 66% in the past two years). Additionally, over 80% (244) of Barossa members are certified, which means they have reached ‘best practice’ authorised by a third-party audit under the internationally recognised Freshcare standard.

The post 90% of Barossa vineyard area now participating in national sustainability program appeared first on Winetitles.
content:
Barossa Australia has revealed that more than 300 Barossa vineyards and wineries are now participating in Sustainable Winegrowing Australia, with over 80% achieving independent certification.

12,768 Ha (90%) of Barossa’s 14,162 Ha under-vine is participating in Sustainable Winegrowing Australia — a 1,264 hectare (10%) increase on the previous year.

303 Barossa vineyards and wineries are now members of the program (an increase of 66% in the past two years). Additionally, over 80% (244) of Barossa members are certified, which means they have reached ‘best practice’ authorised by a third-party audit under the internationally recognised Freshcare standard.

In the past five years, Barossa Australia explained it has obtained three government grants, valued at over $170,000 for the region, to help reduce the cost and administration of the program for growers and winemakers. The organisation said this has “funded free certification training at The Barossa Cellar for 80 businesses, and 30 one-on-one and group sessions with expert local viticulturists to support preparation for audit”.

Beyond the environmental benefits, Barossa Australia viticultural development manager Nicki Robins said participation in Sustainable Winegrowing Australia is increasingly important.

“The significance of reaching 90% of the whole region is that we can communicate Barossa’s collective sustainability credentials with confidence and integrity — from growers at the grassroots, through to wineries and wine brands.

“For growers and wine brands, certification provides independently verified credentials that can help meet growing customer and export market expectations. For consumers, it offers greater confidence in how Barossa wines are produced,” she said.

Barossa Australia shared a few sustainability achievements from the 303 Barossa-based members of the program.

  • 2,405 hectares has been set aside for biodiversity — an increase of 48% since last year
  • 84% of vineyards are at best practice for pest and disease management
  • Only 2% of vineyards have bare soil in the mid-row; 10% plant an annual cover crop, and 88% have a permanent volunteer or native cover crop in the mid-row.

title: Gippsland Wine Show attracts 116 entries, awards seven trophies and 85 medals
summary:
In a record medal tally, the 2026 Farmer’s Daughters Gippsland Wine Show attracted 116 entries “with a strong focus on the region’s famed Pinot Noir and Chardonnay classes”. Wine Gippsland president Rob Lightfoot said there was an “outstanding haul” of 85 medals from the 103 varietal entries yielding seven trophies, “a testament to the exceptional quality of wine in Gippsland”. He thanked the sponsors and partners for their support of an industry that raises the region’s profile and attracts visitors. The 15 gold medals, 31 silver and 39 bronzes were presented at the annual celebration held for 120 guests at Trulli, Meeniyan in South Gippsland.

content:
The trophy winners from the 2026 Gippsland Wine Show. Image supplied

In a record medal tally, the 2026 Farmer’s Daughters Gippsland Wine Show attracted 116 entries “with a strong focus on the region’s famed Pinot Noir and Chardonnay classes”.

Wine Gippsland president Rob Lightfoot said there was an “outstanding haul” of 85 medals from the 103 varietal entries yielding seven trophies, “a testament to the exceptional quality of wine in Gippsland”.

He thanked the sponsors and partners for their support of an industry that raises the region’s profile and attracts visitors.

The 15 gold medals, 31 silver and 39 bronzes were presented at the annual celebration held for 120 guests at Trulli, Meeniyan in South Gippsland.

The Farmer’s Daughters Best Wine of Show went to South Gippsland’s Gippsland Wine Company 2025 Loch Chardonnay. The trophy was presented to Mark Heath and Jane Taylor, who had earlier picked up the coveted Best Chardonnay Top Gold and trophy in a competitive category that produced a record three gold medals, four silver and seven bronze from 16 entries. They also took home the Best Sparkling Gold and Trophy with the GWC 2021 Blanc de Noir.

Heath was delighted with the win, thanking his team and praising the camaraderie of the “family of the Gippsland wine community that supports each other and comes together at the annual awards”.

The judging panel was led by chair of judges Julian Grounds, technical director at Stonier Wines; Max Allen, acclaimed Australian wine journalist and author; and Noah Ward, wine educator and podcast host.

“The outstanding results and sheer number of medals show just what the vintage of 2025 could produce in a region like this,” Grounds said.

In only their second year entering the show, Rory and Jo McKenzie from Bull At A Gate in Pound Creek won the Best Riesling Top Gold and Trophy for the 2026 Riesling. They also took home a gold medal for their 2026 Albarino, making it two gold from two entries and their first time producing single-variety wines.

Blackcoat Wines in Ellinbank won Best Aromatic White Top Gold and Trophy for the Blackcoat 2025 Chenin Blanc.

Andrew and Peter Hatton of French Island Vineyards won Best Shiraz with Gold and Trophy for the French Island Vineyards 2025 Shiraz.

Marcus Satchell and Lisa Sartori of Dirty Three Wines, Inverloch, took home three of the four golds among 29 entries in the Pinot Noir class, winning Top Gold and the Trophy with the Dirty Three ‘Dirt 2’ Pinot Noir. Frank Butera and Bass River Winery was also awarded gold for the Bass River 2025 Pinot Noir 1835. Dirty Three also won gold for the Dirty Three 2025 ‘All The Dirts’ Chardonnay.

Lightfoot Wines won Best Other Red Varieties and Blends with Top Gold for the 2025 Minotaur, presented by East Gippsland Shire. They also picked up a gold medal in the same class with their 2025 Gamay.

Showcasing three vintages of the same wine, Lightfoot Wines was awarded the Best White Wine of Provenance for the Lightfoot Home Block Chardonnay vintages 2024, 2023 and 2021, presented by Annette Spink of Coast magazine.

Waratah Hills Vineyard of Fish Creek was awarded Best Red Wine of Provenance for the Waratah Hills Pinot Noir 2025, 2024 and 2015 vintages, presented to viticulturalist Georgia Roberts by Simon Johnson, CEO of Food & Fibre Gippsland. Waratah Hills also won Best Rosé for the 2026 Pinot Noir Rosé, presented by Sandrine Gimon representing BHF Technologies.

Most Successful Exhibitor was presented to Marcus Satchell of Dirty Three Wines by Simon Kelton of Monacellars.

In only their second year of entering the show, Wandilla Estate, Leongatha, picked up a gold medal for the 2025 Riesling.

Narkoojee Winery, Glengarry North, won gold for the Narkoojee 2022 Reserve Chardonnay.

Other class winners included Blue Gables Vineyard for Best Sauvignon Blanc with its Blue Gables 2026 Sauvignon Blanc and Purple Hen Winery with Best Cabernet Sauvignon for its Purple Hen 2025 Cabernet.

Rob Lightfoot welcomed the representatives of local shires and Wine Victoria CEO Stephanie Duboudin before thanking Julian Grounds and all involved in the show judging as well as awards dinner.

“Like many industries, the wine community has its fair share of challenges. But there will always be a place for wines that are made with integrity and authenticity, by people who genuinely care about the place they grow grapes, and the way that they make the wine,” Lightfoot said.

“That’s not something that can be easily replicated. It is something that we do very well in Gippsland. The depth of quality on display is a confirmation that Gippsland is indeed an excellent place to grow grapes and to make wine.”

Huntington Estate was among the standout performers, named Most Successful Exhibitor at Show and taking out the Most Outstanding Classic Red Blend for its 2023 Grand Reserve Cabernet Sauvignon and Shiraz. Tim Stevens, chief winemaker and owner of Huntington Estate, was also named Winemaker of the Year. Rosby Wines took out Best Wine of Show for its Rosby 2025 Riesling, which also received Best White Wine of Show and Best Riesling in Show.

content:
Tim Stevens of Huntington Estate and Sean Richardson from Nutrien Ag. Image supplied

The 54th CCL Mudgee Wine Show has celebrated another year of outstanding wines and achievements across the Mudgee wine industry, with the 2026 trophy winners announced at the Mudgee Wine Show Awards at Di Lusso Estate on Thursday 10 September.

Huntington Estate was among the standout performers, named Most Successful Exhibitor at Show and taking out the Most Outstanding Classic Red Blend for its 2023 Grand Reserve Cabernet Sauvignon and Shiraz. Tim Stevens, chief winemaker and owner of Huntington Estate, was also named Winemaker of the Year.

Rosby Wines took out Best Wine of Show for its Rosby 2025 Riesling, which also received Best White Wine of Show and Best Riesling in Show.

Stein was another major trophy winner, receiving Best Museum White Wine for its 2019 Riesling, Best Shiraz in Show for its 2024 Preservative Free Organic Shiraz, and the Gil Wahlquist Perpetual Trophy for Best Organic/Biodynamic/Preservative Free Wine.

Heslop Wines took out Best Red Wine of Show for its 2023 Touriga Nacional, which also won the trophy for Best Red Wine other than Shiraz and Cabernet Sauvignon. The winery was also named the Most Successful Small Producer.

Alex Finnie, Mudgee Wine Association member and lead of the Mudgee Wine Show Sub-Committee, said the standard of entries reflected the depth and diversity of the region’s wine industry.

“Once again, the standard of entries in this year’s Mudgee Wine Show was incredibly strong. The three days of judging give our producers an opportunity to have their wines assessed by experienced industry judges and see how they perform alongside some of the region’s best.

“The results are a great reflection of the depth and diversity of our wine industry. From established producers to smaller and emerging winemakers, there are some really exciting wines being made in Mudgee, and the show gives us an opportunity to recognise and celebrate the people behind them.”

The show also “recognised those making a significant contribution to the region’s wine industry”.

McIntosh Estate was named Most Outstanding Cellar Door and received the Vineyard of the Year Award, while Tom Dunstan was recognised with the Rising Star Emerging Leader Award and Paul Baguley received the Jennifer Moncrieff Award for Most Outstanding Contribution to the Mudgee Wine Industry.

As both Mudgee Wine Association president and a Rising Star award recipient, Tom Dunstan said the show was an important opportunity to celebrate the region and its next generation.

“The Mudgee Wine Show is a great opportunity to celebrate the people and wines that make our region so special. I’m proud to see our industry come together and recognise the achievements of our local producers,” Dunstan said.

“On a personal level, receiving the Rising Star Emerging Leader Award is incredibly rewarding. I’ve learnt so much from the people who have come before me and helped shape the Mudgee wine industry. I’m proud to be part of that continuing story and excited to take what I’ve learnt forward and contribute to the next generation of Mudgee wine.”

2026 Mudgee Wine Show Trophy highlights:

  • Winemaker of the Year: Tim Stevens – Huntington Estate
  • Best Wine of Show: Rosby Wines 2025 Riesling
  • Best White Wine of Show: Rosby Wines 2025 Riesling
  • Best Red Wine of Show: Heslop Wines 2023 Touriga Nacional
  • Most Successful Exhibitor: Huntington Estate
  • Most Successful Small Producer: Heslop Wines
  • Most Outstanding Cellar Door: McIntosh Estate
  • Vineyard of the Year: McIntosh Estate
  • Best Riesling: Rosby Wines 2025 Riesling
  • Best Shiraz: Stein 2024 Preservative Free Organic Shiraz
  • Best Cabernet Sauvignon: Heslop Wines 2023 Cabernet Sauvignon
  • Best Classic Red Blend: Huntington Estate 2023 Grand Reserve Cabernet Sauvignon and Shiraz
  • Best Museum White: Stein 2019 Riesling
  • Best Museum Red: Yeates 2018 Reserve Shiraz Cabernet Blend
  • Best White Other Than Chardonnay and Riesling: Grapes of Roth 2026 Sauvignon Blanc
  • Best Red Other Than Shiraz and Cabernet Sauvignon: Heslop Wines 2023 Touriga Nacional
  • Best Organic/Biodynamic/Preservative Free Wine: Stein 2024 Preservative Free Organic Shiraz
  • Rising Star Emerging Leader: Tom Dunstan
  • Most Outstanding Contribution to the Mudgee Wine Industry: Paul Baguley

title: NSW establishes $2.6 million Wine Recovery Program
summary:
The New South Wales Government has established a $2.6 million NSW Wine Recovery Program. The program, which is being funded by the Australian Government and delivered by the NSW Government, “is designed to help build resilience, strengthen regional capability and grow demand for NSW wines”. “The NSW wine industry is a vital part of our regional economy, supporting local jobs, tourism and communities as it produces some of the world’s best wines,” said Minister for Agriculture and Regional NSW Tara Moriarty. “Producers are facing tough conditions, with global oversupply and declining wine consumption putting pressure on the industry and the jobs and communities it supports. The NSW Wine Recovery Program will provide targeted support to help producers respond to these challenges, strengthen the sector and remain competitive.”

The post NSW establishes $2.6 million Wine Recovery Program appeared first on Winetitles.
content:
Minister Tara Moriarty announcing the program at the 2026 NSW Wine Awards. Image supplied

The New South Wales Government has established a $2.6 million NSW Wine Recovery Program.

The program, which is being funded by the Australian Government and delivered by the NSW Government, “is designed to help build resilience, strengthen regional capability and grow demand for NSW wines”.

The state government said the program will be delivered through the following streams of activities:

  • Building regional wine grape and wine producer capability and boosting domestic demand
  • Provide financial assistance to eligible industry organisations representing winegrape growers and wine producers in NSW through grants.
  • Grants of $20,000 to $100,000 available to strengthen regional industry capability including developing regional and emerging leadership, mental health and business resilience programs, and building the capability of winegrape and wine producers.
  • Grants of $20,000 to $250,000 available to boost demand for NSW wine through consumer-focused campaigns promoting NSW wine regions, domestic familiarisation visits, and support for industry participation at trade shows and events.

“The NSW wine industry is a vital part of our regional economy, supporting local jobs, tourism and communities as it produces some of the world’s best wines,” said Minister for Agriculture and Regional NSW Tara Moriarty.

“Producers are facing tough conditions, with global oversupply and declining wine consumption putting pressure on the industry and the jobs and communities it supports.

“The NSW Wine Recovery Program will provide targeted support to help producers respond to these challenges, strengthen the sector and remain competitive.”

NSW Wine has welcomed the announcement, saying it has “consistently advocated to the NSW Premier, Minister for Agriculture and relevant NSW Ministers for direct and targeted industry support”.

“While we recognise this grant alone will not solve every issue facing businesses across the state, it is a positive step and clear acknowledgement from the NSW Government of the value our industry adds to the NSW economy and the importance of your businesses to the fabric of regional life,” said NSW Wine president Mark Bourne.

“NSW Wine will continue advocating on the broader issues affecting our members.”

More information on the grants including eligibility, inclusion and exclusions is available here.

Applications are already open and will remain so until 4pm 27 November 2026.

content:
All of the trophy winners at the 2026 Margaret River Wine Show. Images credit Ovis Creative

The 2026 Endeavour Group Margaret River Wine Show, held on Wadandi Boodja, culminated in a Gala Awards Lunch at Aravina Estate on Friday 30 October, celebrating the region’s finest wines and producers.

The Mandoon Estate Wilyabrup Cabernet Sauvignon 2023 was awarded Wine of Show, receiving four trophies, and a fifth for Mandoon Estate as Most Successful Exhibitor:

  • Endeavour Group Trophy for Wine of Show
  • Pellenc Trophy for Red Wine of Show
  • Tonnellerie de Mercurey Trophy for Best Single Vineyard Red
  • City of Busselton Trophy for Best Cabernet Sauvignon
  • Vinline Mobile Bottling Trophy for Most Successful Exhibitor

“I couldn’t be prouder of what we’re able to do in Margaret River. Our winemaking team is led by Ryan Sudano and it bamboozles me what he and the team do. We encourage and drive passion in our people, and that’s led from our owner Allan Erceg,” said Andrew Pruyn, general manager at Mandoon Estate.

“There’s a reason why we’ve invested so heavily in Margaret River — we can’t get fruit of the quality anywhere else, the region is just so strong with what it’s able to produce. It is a big part of our business, and we’re incredibly grateful. Thanks to all the committee and congratulations to all the other winners.”

David Bicknell chaired the judging panel for the third consecutive year, alongside an international judge, eight national and local judges, and six associates.

Margaret River Wine Association (MRWA) CEO Penny Dickeson said the committee, led by co-chairs 2025 Len Evans Dux Andrew Bretherton (Juniper Estate) and Matt Godfrey (Cherubino) had assembled an exceptional group of judges.

“We are pleased to once again welcome an impressive, highly-experienced and diverse set of judges to Margaret River for the 2026 wine show, including five Len Evans Tutorial Scholars — three of them Dux of their cohort.”

The panel assessed over 580 entries from 87 exhibitors at the Margaret River Heart, awarding 57 gold, 81 silver, and 215 bronze medals — a medal strike rate of over 62%.

“Margaret River is an unusual wine show because the number of high-quality exhibits exceeds almost every other show in the country, including the National Wine Show,” said David Bicknell.

“It’s your work, it’s not mine — I’m just endorsing it. The percentage of golds in the show has hit 10%, that’s double the national average from all major shows, it’s quite extraordinary.”

The international judge was Hong Kong-based Corrine Mui of Corvino Asia, who said the Chardonnay showed “remarkable tension, intensity and refinement”.

“So much energy. That makes this place amongst the best Chardonnay regions on the planet,” Mui continued.

“Coming from Asia, I know how much opportunity exists for Margaret River on the global stage. I understand the modern consumer or the younger generation nowadays may prefer some lighter bodied reds. Cabernet may seem difficult to sell, but Asia still drinks a considerable amount of Cabernet so you can come over to our part of the world…we drink so much Cabernet!”

The Lifetime Achievement Award was presented to Clare and Keith Mugford of Moss Wood, “recognising their four decades of outstanding winemaking, and pivotal role in shaping Margaret River wine, globally”.

“The Margaret River Lifetime Achievement Award is peer-nominated by the local industry. Clare and Keith Mugford, as winemakers, viticulturists and proprietors of Moss Wood, have made consistent, highly acclaimed Margaret River wines over four decades, and are amongst the longest-serving winemakers of any fine-wine estate in Australia,” said Peter Campbell, chair of the Margaret River Wine Association.

“Under their leadership, Moss Wood wines, and the Moss Wood Cabernet Sauvignon in particular, have become Australian benchmarks, celebrated for exceptional quality, consistency and longevity.”

Moss Wood was the second vineyard planted in Margaret River in 1969 by Dr Bill and Sandra Pannell. In 1979, Roseworthy College graduate Keith Mugford arrived at Moss Wood to take up the role of winemaker and viticulturist.

Clare joined Keith Mugford at Moss Wood in 1984, and the couple became managing partners of the business. In 1985, they acquired Moss Wood from the Pannell family.

“We are thrilled, honoured and humbled to have our contribution to the region and to Margaret River viticulture and winemaking recognised with this award. Thank you,” said Clare and Keith Mugford.

summary:
The trophies from the 2026 MGA Insurance Group McLaren Vale Wine Show, including Best Wine of Show and the prestigious ‘Bushing Monarch’ title, were awarded at the 53rd annual McLaren Vale Bushing Lunch on Friday 30 October. The Big Easy Radio 2025 Perpetual Holidaze Grenache was named Best Wine of Show for 2026, crowning owner and winemaker Matt Head as the 2026 McLaren Vale Bushing Monarch. From 652 entries, the Big Easy Radio 2025 Perpetual Holidaze Grenache was awarded the highest accolade by the panel of judges including chair of judges Toby Barlow (Wine SX), international judge Richard Hemming MW (JancisRobinson.com) as well as panel chairs Glenn Barry (Tonic Wines), Steven Paul (Oakdene Vineyards) and Stuart Hordern (Brokenwood Wines).

The post McLaren Vale Wine Show 2026 trophy winners revealed appeared first on Winetitles.
content:
Big Easy Radio co-owners and ‘Bushing Monarchs’ Dr Bianca Price and Matt Head. Image credit Ben Macmahon

The trophies from the 2026 MGA Insurance Group McLaren Vale Wine Show, including Best Wine of Show and the prestigious ‘Bushing Monarch’ title, were awarded at the 53rd annual McLaren Vale Bushing Lunch on Friday 30 October.

The Big Easy Radio 2025 Perpetual Holidaze Grenache was named Best Wine of Show for 2026, crowning owner and winemaker Matt Head as the 2026 McLaren Vale Bushing Monarch.

From 652 entries, the Big Easy Radio 2025 Perpetual Holidaze Grenache was awarded the highest accolade by the panel of judges including chair of judges Toby Barlow (Wine SX), international judge Richard Hemming MW (JancisRobinson.com) as well as panel chairs Glenn Barry (Tonic Wines), Steven Paul (Oakdene Vineyards) and Stuart Hordern (Brokenwood Wines).

“Grenache was, as expected, a highlight and continues to be such an exciting and compelling story within Australian wine. However, the depth and expression across Shiraz wines also promoted a lot of discussion between judges and stiff competition for trophies. The standout trend in Shiraz was balance and freshness while sitting alongside Mclaren Vale’s trademark palate generosity,” said Barlow.

“This year’s show was also a poignant reminder of why this region continues to raise the bar for Mediterranean varieties in Australia. Many of the wines showed real confidence and varietal understanding from growers and winemakers in tune with their vineyard sites and climate.

The emerging varieties continue to positively develop across both red and whites and are becoming an integral part of the McLaren Vale narrative. The authentic fit between these varieties, their styles, the regional venues and outstanding food offering really elevates both the wine quality potential, but importantly the consumer experience too.”

Barlow emphasised that the Best Wine of Show vote was very close this year, however, the winning Grenache “just kept showing up and growing from the very first bracket”.

“It’s both modern and classic at the same time, and very compelling. On top of that every element was in balance, nothing out of place, with a finish that kept drawing the judges back. It captures McLaren Vale at its very best,” he concluded.

Visiting international judge Richard Hemming MW, head of creative, Asia for JancisRobinson.com, offered his global perspective to the judging.

“As expected, the Grenache, Shiraz and Cabernet Sauvignon wines were standouts, demonstrating the region’s aptitude for both compelling diversity and outstanding quality,” Hemming said.

He described his experience judging at the McLaren Vale Wine Show as “a seriously fun responsibility”.

“The work is no joke: hundreds of wines are scrutinised by multiple tasters in multiple stages to ensure that the very best efforts gain recognition. But the atmosphere is light-hearted, and the energy is nothing but positive. As an international judge, it was an honour to take part. And the results speak for themselves, demonstrating a level of excellence that makes McLaren Vale one of Australia’s most exciting and dynamic wine regions.”

McLaren Vale Wine Region CEO Erin Leggat reflected that the 2026 McLaren Vale Wine Show quality was exceptional.

“Around one in ten wines received a gold medal, with Grenache and Shiraz leading the field and varieties like Fiano and Nero d’Avola now standing up in their own right. These results confirm what trade and consumers increasingly know: McLaren Vale is producing some of the most distinctive and consistently high-quality wine in Australia.

“To see such depth across Shiraz, Grenache and our Mediterranean varieties, tells you this region isn’t standing still. Our growers and winemakers are refining what they do best and backing the varieties that suit our climate and our future,” Leggat said.
